query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a liquid‐metal dealloying step in processing molten Cu with a Ti-containing precursor will selectively remove Ti-rich interdendritic channels to yield an aligned RHEA–Cu phase, which increases the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite while retaining its mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally synthesized W–Cu composite produced via standard powder metallurgy or casting methods, containing a homogeneous distribution of W and Cu phases.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a liquid‐metal dealloying step in a molten Cu processing route where Ti-rich interdendritic channels in a pre-alloyed precursor are selectively dissolved. This results in an aligned RHEA (refractory high-entropy alloy) phase embedded within the Cu matrix.
generation.conditions: The intervention is designed for composites used in high-heat flux and fusion-reactor joint applications, where operational temperatures and irradiation levels mimic those in advanced heat-dissipation and fusion reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of aligned RHEA features within the Cu matrix acts as a structural mediator that enhances Cu connectivity and creates more direct thermal conduction pathways while reinforcing the composite structurally.
generation.mechanism: The selective removal of Ti-rich channels through liquid-metal dealloying promotes the formation of a continuous, aligned conductive phase (RHEA–Cu) that enhances thermal transport. Meanwhile, the RHEA phase contributes to mechanical robustness and irradiation resistance, thereby maintaining the composite’s overall durability under extreme conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite produced by conventional routes, the liquid-metal dealloyed composite is predicted to exhibit a higher thermal conductivity (with an anticipated relative improvement that may be on the order of 10–20%, though the exact value is uncertain) while matching the mechanical durability and irradiation resistance required for high-performance applications.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics of a standard W–Cu composite manufactured without the liquid-metal dealloying step serve as the baseline.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold within the temperature and irradiation regimes typical of advanced heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications. Extreme variations outside these conditions may affect the effectiveness of the dealloying process and the stability of the resulting microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thermal conductivity enhancement and the long-term stability of the RHEA–Cu alignment under operational irradiation and thermal cycling remain uncertain until systematic experimental validation is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set using the conventional processing route and a second set incorporating the liquid-metal dealloying intervention. Subject both sets to standard thermal cycling and simulated fusion reactor irradiation conditions. Compare the composites’ thermal conductivity, mechanical durability (e.g., via stress-strain testing), and irradiation resistance (e.g., via post-irradiation microstructural analysis).
measurements: Thermal conductivity (using laser flash analysis or similar)
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM imaging under irradiation conditions)
Irradiation resistance (quantifying defect density or phase stability post-irradiation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the liquid-metal dealloyed composite does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity relative to the baseline, or if mechanical durability and irradiation resistance are compromised (falling below the performance metrics of the baseline composite), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
